evidence: Cic. Amic. 88: sī aliquem cui narrāret habuisset
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: aliquis says that someone exists, though it does not matter who; quis leaves even that open; quīdam is someone the speaker knows but does not name.

terms.gloss: someone, anyone (after sī, nisi, num, nē)
evidence: Cic. Sen. 83: sī quis deus mihi largiātur
Cic. Amic. 88: sī quis in caelum ascendisset

terms.gloss: anyone (after a negative, and in questions that expect “no”)
evidence: Cic. Sen. 21: nec vērō quemquam senem audīvī oblītum
terms.comment: “Not anyone” is nēmō, “and no one” nec quisquam (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Amph. 1020: heus, ecquis hīc est?

terms.gloss: someone, a certain person (known but not named)
evidence: Cic. Clu. 177: quīdam ex advocātīs (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: someone or other, something or other
terms.grammar: nesciō with an indefinite: “I know not who”; it does not change the mood of the verb
evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. nesciō: “I know not who, some one, somebody, a certain person”
Traupman 190: Nesciō quis senātor, some senator or other

phrases.latin: Heus, heus. Ecquis hīc? Ego sum Chremēs.
phrases.english: Hello, hello! Is anyone there? It’s me, Chremes.

phrases.latin: nec vērō quemquam senem audīvī oblītum quō locō thēsaurum obruisset
phrases.english: and I never heard of any old man who forgot where he had buried his treasure

phrases.latin: sī quis in caelum ascendisset nātūramque mundī et pulchritūdinem sīderum perspexisset, īnsuāvem illam admīrātiōnem eī fore; quae jūcundissima fuisset, sī aliquem cui narrāret habuisset
phrases.english: if someone went up into heaven and saw the nature of the universe and the beauty of the stars, the wonder of it would give him no pleasure; it would have been the sweetest thing if he had had someone to tell
